newsitem.title: UK: Soft euro better than no euro, bond markets signal.
newsitem.headline: Soft euro better than no euro, bond markets signal.

text.p: Hard or soft, bond markets are betting on single European currency union going ahead as planned in 1999, analysts said on Wednesday.
Bond investors were rattled by the left's surprise win in the first round of French elections on Sunday, but convergence trades were soon back on track.
Longer term, however, a soft euro means higher interest rates and would likely weigh on financial markets, especially if heavy borrowers like Italy squeezed in from the beginning, analysts said.

"The French elections makes everything a bit uncertain and though the EMU process has gone too far to be dropped, the markets are now discounting a wider group of countries joining EMU," said Elisabeth Asseth at broker Williams de Broe.
In the short term, a weak single currency in Europe could help to solidify economic recovery and foster trade between European bond markets in which yields were converging, analysts said.

"People think a euro is an inevitable thing and if that means it's a weak euro, so be it," said Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam."If that's the case, you may as well profit from the (bond) spreads."
The entry requirements laid down by the Maastricht Treaty for European economic and monetary union (EMU) are tough.
Public deficit, for instance, must not exceed three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and total debt must not go above 60 percent of GDP.
Such high standards would seem to push Italy out of the picture for joining in the first round.
But as more and more EMU-candidates juggle their books to find extra cash, there are increasing signs that entry rules may be relaxed to achieve a broader single currency area.
French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin favours a flexible approach to the Maastrich criteria. Analysts say if he wins the second round on Sunday, the future of EMU may be thrown further into doubt.
Spreads against Bunds widened late on Wednesday as the mark lept against other European currencies amid nervousness before Sunday's second round of elections.
But analyst do not expect an unravelling of the convergence that has been a feature of European bond markets since 1995.

The spread between Italian and German 10-year bond yields has narrowed sharply from around 475 basis points at the beginning of 1996 and many bond experts expect it to narrow further towards 100 by next year from 140 basis points now.
"If Italy is included then it is unlikely to require a credit spread of 130 basis points," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London.
But a key concern is that Germany, which is spearheading the move toward EMU, may not want to swap the mark -- regarded as a bulwark against inflation, for a weak euro.
"The risk is if the euro is regarded as weak, the German people won't sign up to it," said Edmonds.
Germany's own intentions to tap Bundesbank reserves to plug a revenue shortfall has further fuelled market jitters over EMU.
Such concerns have been cause for a higher risk premium attached to German Bunds, while the mark was expected to weaken longer term.
Analysts said 10-year Bund yields could spike higher from their current level of around six percent, reversing the direction of yield convergence with peripheral bonds.
The prospect of tighter credit in the United States, possibly in July, would also weigh on German yields.
